Is the site located within the downwind horizontal influence distance from the
crest?
(i.e., is X in step (B7) < influence distance?)

Yes: Go to step (B10)
No: Local topography for downwind is not significant. No further
calculation is necessary. Take the topography factor S, = 1.

Determine the length of the downwind slope Lp in the wind direction by
Lp = H/ ap.

Determine the effective slope a according to the steepness of the upwind slope
ay determined in step (B1):

If ay is not greater than 0.3, @ = Qu
If ay is greater than 0.3, a. = 0.3

Determine the effective slope length L, according to the steepness of the
upwind slope ay determined in step (B1):

If ay is not greater than 0.3, Le = Lu
If ay is greater than 0.3, L. = H/0.3

Calculate the distance ratio X/Lp in the case of “hill-and-ridge” topography, or
X/L, in the case of “cliff-and-escarpment” topography. (A/Lp or X/Le is
positive with respect to wind direction B.)

Determine the topography location factor s for various height z above ground:

For “hill-and-ridge” topography:

Obtain s from the downwind side (right-hand side) of Figure C3 in the Code,
according to the height ratio z/L, and the distance ratio X/Lp.

For “cliff-and-escarpment” topography:

Obtain s from the downwind side (right-hand side) of Figure C4 in the Code,
according to the height ratio z/L, and the distance ratio X/Le.

Calculate the topography factor S, for various height z above ground, by the
following equation:

S, =(1+1.2a,s)

In Figures C3 and C4 of the Code, the height above ground ratio is in log scale and the
horizontal position ratio is in natural scale. Figures C3 and C4 of the Code are
reproduced in figure 3.2 and figure 3.3 respectively, with minor grids added for user’s
convenience.

Example calculations of topography factors are given in calculation sheets 3.1, 3.2
and 3.3.
